sentences.sentence: What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?" [1] The four are conventionally named enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal, and the sequence of the questions is not a sequence in time.

Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order." [1] That simultaneity matters for how the tetrad can be assessed.
Obsolescence names what the new form pushes aside, and retrieval names an older form it brings back; both are about the relation between the new medium and what came before it [1].
Reversal is conditional: it describes what happens "when pushed to extremes", not what happens next [1].
It quotes *Laws of Media* (p. 116) calling the tetrad a tool for exploring the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool for describing situations in process rather than settled ones [1].
He records that the introduction calls the laws "the single biggest intellectual discovery of the last couple of centuries" [15].
On page 7 of the same book they are described as a "heuristic" device "that allows for adjustments and implementations" [15].
Guardiani also reports William Kuhns's reading of the four slots as "the metaphysical coda of McLuhan's career" [15].
On that reading the tetrad is the summary statement of a body of work rather than a method inside it [15].

Michael Bolton's "McLuhan for Testers" column in *Better Software* (October 2007) tells software testers that "McLuhan proposed that every medium can be submitted to fourprobes—testing heuristics— that he called the Laws of Media" [13].

He then puts them to a requirement, a feature or an organisational change: what does it extend, what does it obsolesce, what earlier medium does it retrieve, and how does it reverse when stretched [13].
The phone's retrieval question surfaces the Pony Express, the all-in-one printer-scanner-fax and the Tamagotchi [13].
Its reversal question surfaces interrupted conversation and the desk that follows you everywhere [13].
None of them tells the analyst how much of an effect counts, over what period, or against what baseline [1].
Guardiani's survey records John Sturrock's verdict that "The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing" [15].
It also records John Fekete's objection that the number four is treated as a "metaphysically privileged explanatory structure", with no grounds given for privileging it [15].

The opening of *Laws of Media* states it directly: "This essay offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws) observations about the structure and nature of things man makes and does" [7].
The publisher's description follows the book's own framing, calling the four laws "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [8].

The same publisher's text contains the sentence that undoes the claim: "Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation." [8] If answering all four is a condition of being a human artefact at all, then no artefact can fail the tetrad.

Eduardo Basbaum, writing in *ARS* (2019), argues the tetrad fails Popper's own criterion in the way Popper said Freudian psychoanalysis fails it: "It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands, since its testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper dismisses Freudian psychoanalysis theory: it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim." [7] A scheme that always works explains nothing, because it excludes nothing.

Long thought to be “plans” or “blueprints,” it is found to be situational or environmental cause and to operate in many fields, particularly the arts, and the study of media and their ecologies." [11] On this reading the tetrad does not predict what a maker will do.
Library and Archives Canada states flatly that "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool" [1].
The custodian of McLuhan's papers presents the four laws as an exploratory instrument, not as the new science the book's title announces [1].
His intent was to probe—to investigate and explore ideas with think- ing tools that included metaphor, paradox, and even satire" [10].
The four laws are asserted to hold simultaneously, and Library and Archives Canada concedes that McLuhan himself sometimes spoke of them as succeeding each other [1].
The tetrad is also offered as universally applicable, to any artefact at any time [8].
That universality makes it valuable as a probe, and makes it unfalsifiable as a law [8].

Thomas Hylland Eriksen, at the University of Oslo, applied the tetrad to the Internet in 1996 and treated the four laws as a starting point rather than a result: "Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out." [4] He filled in tetrads for CD-ROM, the LP, the aeroplane and the Internet.
He called the results "questionable" illustrations whose value was in forcing distinctions between technological, social and cultural levels of effect [4].

The Internet tetrad is the most revealing thing in his paper: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics." [4] A scheme that assigns the same phenomenon to all four slots is being used as a set of prompts, not as a set of claims about the world.

Isabelle Adam's 2016 paper in *Glocality* applies the tetrad to the smartphone, and her defence of the method is its universality rather than its accuracy: "Although McLuhan developed the tetrad three decades ago, it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments." [3] The filled-in result treats enhancement as access and speed, obsolescence as feature phones, personal computers and home printers, and retrieval as cameras and books: "The smartphone enhances the accessibility and convenience of the medium internet, which also accelerates the speed of real-time communication." [3] Adam concedes the interpretive latitude explicitly: "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions." [3] She also claims only that the tetrad lets the analyst "try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [3].

Logan argues that "despite McLuhan’s claim not to have a theory of communication that in fact the body of his work does indeed constitute a theory of media and their effects which I have called his General Theory of Media (GToM) that also includes his Laws of Media (LoM)" [14].

McLuhan’s notion of law as used in his Laws of Media; ii. the notions of the Law in the legal sense and iii. the notion of law as formulated in scientific laws." [14] That comparison, from the most sympathetic systematiser, concedes that the tetrad's "law" is not the scientific kind.
"The Missing Media Laws," by Marshall and Eric McLuhan, was published in *Explorations in Media Ecology* volume 6, issue 3, in September 2007, pages 197 to 202 [9].
It appeared in a media-ecology journal, which is where the tetrad's unpublished material has appeared since [9].

Bolton's *Better Software* column is the clearest specimen: it treats a test team as a medium, argues the team enhances the project's ability to learn about the product, obsolesces the field technician and the careful developer, and reverses into the team not reporting what it finds [13].
The team also retrieves an older role, which Bolton names as the test pilot, the food taster, the editor and the lab researcher [13].
Takkeci and Erdem's 2024 study of online architectural studios during the pandemic screened 176 records and coded 20 empirical papers [2].

The coding scheme was not the tetrad: the authors sorted the findings under four studio archetypes, and only then read them through the tetrad — "This process was followed by organizing the findings and interpreting them within the tetradic framework" [2].

A single finding then does multiple duty: "Hence, the idea of the community of practices reversed into isolated individuals, and the multidimensional communication of the studio was obsolesced, and this retrieved the master apprenticeship pedagogy because the tutor ended up as the only actor through whom all the exchanges happen" [2].
The authors assign three quadrants to that one observed shift, after the fact [2].
The authors' own framing concedes the point: "McLuhan’s ideas on media can be viewed as an evolutionary theory that needs to be re-evaluated with each technological transformation." [2]
Venable's "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and McLuhan's reply, "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" [5].
He reports Eric McLuhan's claim in *Laws of Media* that the questions can be asked, and the answers checked, by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact [6].
His answer is flat: "This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans’ own examples illustrates." [6] The illustration is the book's own inconsistency.

The second version: "In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult." [6] Tyler draws the inference: "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad’s application, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by “anyone, anywhere, at any time”." [6] Reproducibility fails at the source, before any external replication is attempted.

At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps." [6] The looseness means any set of answers can be defended; the rigidity means answers must be produced even where the evidence is absent.

Basbaum's 2019 *ARS* article makes the comparison to psychoanalysis, though as a debatable judgement rather than a verdict: "It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands" [7].
Basbaum argues that it probably cannot be refuted, since it "seems to always work" [7].
Eric McLuhan's formal-cause framing gives this position a philosophical footing: the laws describe "situational or environmental cause" rather than a maker's plan [11].
The defence has a cost, which is that it gives up the testability claim the book opens with [7].
In 1976 a critic published "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and McLuhan replied that the laws had been misunderstood [5].
By 1988 the publisher was advertising the book as testable while also saying that anything without answers to the four questions "is not the product of human creation" [8].
By 2007 the most careful critic could treat the tetrad as a valuable probe that is not science [6].
By 2016 an applier could describe its output as "at least speculation" without embarrassment [3].

Takkeci and Erdem (2024) screened 176 records on online architectural studios during the pandemic and read 20 empirical papers, coding them under studio archetypes before interpreting the results through the tetrad [2][2].

The authors state the framework's basis plainly: "As referred to in this paper, the functionality of the tetrad is not based on theoretical grounds, but revolves around four questions based on empirical observation" [2].
The paper's limitations section concedes the ceiling: the review "relied solely on previously published research" and generated no new measurements [2].

Adam's smartphone paper states that "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions." [3] A test needs a coding rule independent analysts can apply to the same artefact, and a measure of whether they agree.

Bolton's restatement makes the timing explicit: reversal effects "are emergent; they may be apparent immediately, or they may not be realized until the figure fades into the ground and becomes ubiquitous." [10] A prediction that a medium will flip into its opposite at some unspecified point cannot be scored as right or wrong at any particular date.
The publisher's own description says that anything which does not contain answers to the four questions "is not the product of human creation" [8].

Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu and Daniel Wegner's four studies in *Science* (2011) found that when people expect future access to information, they recall less of the content and more of where to find it [12].
The authors frame it through transactive memory, not the tetrad, and it tests one effect on memory rather than the four laws [12].
The key effect did not replicate in the 2018 Camerer et al. multi-study project covering 21 studies from *Nature* and *Science* [17].
Hesselmann's 2020 study, designed to follow Sparrow's own methodological advice, also found no evidence [17].
The original also had unresolved statistical problems: unclear sample size, post hoc word selection and single-trial measures [17].
Reversal claims are the hardest, because the theory does not say when the flip occurs [10].
Tyler's argument that the tetrad is a probe rather than a science converts it from a claim into a procedure for generating claims [6].

One 2018 conference paper shows the teaching use: "This paper summarizes how the McLuhan Tetrad help the students to handle the laser cleaning technique as a case of study." [18] The smartphone paper is the same pattern in research form, structuring an assessment whose substance comes from elsewhere [3].

notes.quote: McLuhan phrased them as questions with which to consider any artefact: 1. What does it enhance? 2. What does it make obsolete? 3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier? 4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?
notes.claim: Library and Archives Canada gives the canonical four-question wording of the tetrad as published in Laws of Media (1988), phrased as questions applicable to any artefact.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: LAC states the four laws operate simultaneously rather than sequentially, and quotes McLuhan (Laws of Media p. 116) calling the tetrad a tool for exploring the "grammar and syntax" of artefacts rather than a scientific tool.

notes.quote: As referred to in this paper, the functionality of the tetrad is not based on theoretical grounds, but revolves around four questions based on empirical observation
notes.claim: Even a sympathetic 2024 peer-reviewed application treats the tetrad as resting on "empirical observation" rather than on testable theory: the four questions are a lens for interpreting already-existing empirical findings, not a hypothesis with specified outcomes that could be refuted.

notes.quote: This study specifically focused on peer-reviewed, empirical research published after 2020, and the authors used search terms related to online architectural studios during the pandemic. The process identified 176 records of peer-reviewed empirical studies for further analysis and 20 papers were read and included in the review
notes.claim: The closest thing found to an "empirical" tetrad study is Takkeci and Erdem's 2024 systematic review: 176 records screened, 20 empirical papers coded into themes and then sorted into the four tetrad slots. The tetrad organises other researchers' empirical data; it is not itself the object of measurement.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: In the published application to the smartphone (Glocality, 2016), the author concedes that any medium's tetrad admits multiple interpretations grounded in the analyst's own perceptions — no coding rules, inter-coder reliability or disconfirming condition is offered, which is what an empirical test would require.

notes.quote: Additionally, the tetrad allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments.
notes.claim: Predictive status is explicitly downgraded: the tetrad is said to allow reflection and, "at least", speculation about the future — the strongest predictive claim made in a typical post-1988 application, and it comes with no accuracy criterion or scoring rule.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen's 1996 trial application states the testable-worthy claim in the weakest form: the laws are "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and worth trying out only as a way of creating distinctions between kinds of effects, needing supplementing.

notes.quote: While all the above is questionable and certainly merits to be treated in greater detail, the application of McLuhan's tetrad indicates the necessity to distinguish between different kinds of effects of technologies at the sociocultural level.
notes.claim: Eriksen's own filled-in tetrads for CD-ROM, the LP, the aeroplane and the Internet are presented as "questionable" illustrations whose value lies in prompting distinctions (technological/social/cultural levels), not in verified prediction — and he notes the tetrad can be filled with contradictory content (the Internet "intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics").

notes.claim: The 1976 Technology and Culture exchange is a two-part item: Venable's critique "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (DOI 10.2307/3103072, author W. H. Venable, 1976) and McLuhan's own reply, published as "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" (DOI 10.2307/3103073, author listed as M. McLuhan, 1976) — i.e. McLuhan answered the critic in the same journal, and the reply's title itself frames the critic as having misunderstood the laws.

notes.quote: Although McLuhan developed the tetrad three decades ago, it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments. Its value is also constituted in the concept of bringing four laws together, and thus, looking simultaneously at the past, present, and future, as well as the characteristics of the medium itself and its context.
notes.claim: A post-1988 extension of the tetrad: Isabelle Adam (Glocality, 2016, peer-reviewed journal) applies the tetrad to the smartphone, insisting it is "universal in nature" and still applicable — while conceding "multiple interpretations are possible," which supports the charge that tetrad application is interpretive rather than testable.

notes.quote: Additionally, the tetrad allows one to reflect the past and to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments.
notes.claim: Even a sympathetic applier frames the tetrad's forward use as prediction "or at least speculation" — showing that post-1988 applications treat the tetrad as an interpretive heuristic, not tested predictive science.

notes.quote: His son, Eric McLuhan, even suggests in Laws of Media: The New Science, co-written with his father, that “they can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact” [21]. This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans’ own examples illustrates.
notes.claim: Tyler states the McLuhans' own scientific claim in order to reject it: McLuhan asserted the laws were testable hypotheses and a scientific method modelled on Popper's falsifiability, and Eric McLuhan claimed anyone anywhere could check the answers — Tyler answers flatly that this is not the case.

notes.quote: In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult. If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad’s application, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by “anyone, anywhere, at any time”.
notes.claim: Tyler's killer evidence is internal inconsistency: on the same page of Laws of Media the McLuhans give two incompatible tetrads for wine, which destroys the claim that results are reproducible by anyone anywhere.

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit. At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps.
notes.claim: Tyler's core objection is a double bind, not mere vagueness: as a universal scientific method the tetrad is too loose to be falsified (any creative mind can stretch examples to fit) and simultaneously too rigid, Procrustes-like, because it compels the analyst to fill all four slots whether or not the evidence supports them — so it fails as science in both directions at once.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen (University of Oslo) applied the tetrad to the Internet in 1996, treating the "overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media" as a starting-point that "needs supplementing" — an early post-1988 extension that simultaneously flags the determinism problem.

notes.quote: The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics.
notes.claim: Eriksen's extension of the tetrad to the Internet produces an openly paradoxical result — "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" — showing how a flexible four-part scheme can absorb contradictory findings, which is the basis of critics' Procrustean objection.

notes.quote: The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: Library and Archives Canada's official McLuhan exhibition presents the tetrad as an exploratory instrument rather than a scientific one — i.e., the institutional/curatorial reading retreats from the 'New Science' claim, citing Laws of Media p. 116.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order.
notes.claim: The claimed status of the four laws rests on simultaneity (all four hold at once for any artefact), yet the archive concedes McLuhan himself sometimes spoke of them as successive — an unresolved ambiguity in the doctrine's structure.

notes.quote: Even if, the way I see it, such demonstrations should not be necessary, since changes in culture and society clearly testify, by themselves, how right he was.
notes.claim: Even a sympathetic scholar (Basbaum) ends by dispensing with empirical demonstration: cultural change is said to testify "by itself" — an example of the retreat from testability to self-evidence, and he concedes "the measurability of McLuhan's theory through NCC observation becomes highly undermined."

notes.quote: The laws identified by the McLuhans consitute a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction.
notes.claim: The publisher's own description of Laws of Media asserts the strong status claim: a "new scientific basis for media studies," testable and predictive. (Note: "consitute" is the page's spelling.)

notes.quote: Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation.
notes.claim: The four laws are stated as definitional necessities: every human artefact necessarily answers all four questions, and anything that does not is not human-made. This is the structure that makes the tetrad unfalsifiable — no artefact can fail the test.

notes.quote: By Marshall McLuhan and Eric McLuhan Source: Explorations in Media Ecology, Volume 6, Issue 3, Sep 2007, p. 197 - 202
notes.claim: Post-1988 publication of previously unreleased McLuhan tetrad material: "The Missing Media Laws" by Marshall McLuhan and Eric McLuhan appeared in Explorations in Media Ecology vol. 6, issue 3 (Sept 2007), pp. 197–202 — a precursor stream to the 2017 collection The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan, showing the media-ecology journal circuit as the vehicle for extending the canon.

notes.quote: The smartphone enhances the accessibility and convenience of the medium internet, which also accelerates the speed of real-time communication. Concerning obsolescence, the smartphone pushes feature mobile phones aside as well as decreasing the use of personal computers and home printers. The smartphone retrieves the use of cameras and (e-)books, reviving the linear focus on the medium.
notes.claim: A practical applied-tetrad case from a peer-reviewed journal: the smartphone tetrad (enhancement of internet access and memory; obsolescence of feature phones, PCs and printers; retrieval of camera and book; reversal into augmented reality and interaction-restricting addiction) — an example of the tetrad's post-1988 use as a checklist for technology assessment, including its harms.

report.body:
## TL;DR

McLuhan's tetrad is four questions asked of any artefact: what it enhances, what it obsolesces, what it retrieves, and what it reverses into when pushed to extremes [1]. The McLuhans offered it as testable, falsifiable science in Popper's sense. They also defined it so that no human artefact could fail it, and on a single page of *Laws of Media* they gave two incompatible tetrads for wine [7][8][6]. Scholarship since 1988 has applied and extended the tetrad while steadily demoting it to a heuristic, and no controlled test of the four laws was found. The one rigorous experimental test of a tetrad-style claim, that expecting future access to information changes what people remember, failed replication [12][17]. How sure: very likely no such test exists; the wine example and the wording of the four questions are shown directly.

## Key Findings

- The four laws are stated as questions applicable to any artefact, held to operate simultaneously rather than in sequence [1]. McLuhan himself sometimes spoke of them as successive, an ambiguity the archive concedes [1].
- The McLuhans claimed scientific status in explicit Popperian terms: "This essay offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws)" [7]. The publisher's description of the same book calls the laws "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [8].
- The same description makes the answers definitional: anything without answers to the four questions "is not the product of human creation" [8]. A claim that nothing can fail is not falsifiable in the sense the authors invoked.
- Reviewers saw this on publication. A survey of roughly thirty reviews records John Sturrock's verdict that "The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing" and John Fekete's objection that the number four is treated as a "metaphysically privileged explanatory structure" [15].
- Tom Tyler's critique is a double bind, not a vagueness charge: the tetrad is too loose to be falsified and too rigid to leave a quadrant empty, "it requires us to fill the gaps" [6]. His evidence is internal — two different wine tetrads on one page of *Laws of Media* [6].
- Sympathetic users retreat to heuristic status. Eriksen called the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and produced an Internet tetrad assigning identity politics to all four slots [4]. Adam's smartphone paper concedes that "multiple interpretations are possible" and offers prediction "or at least speculation" [3].
- Extension has been real but non-cumulative. Logan's General Theory of Media compares McLuhan's "law" to legal and scientific law [14]. Harman extends the tetrad to all objects, and later work follows him on screens. Unpublished tetrads keep appearing in media-ecology journals [9]. Practitioners use the four questions in software testing [13].
- No controlled test of the four laws was found. The nearest thing is a 2024 review that coded 20 empirical papers under studio archetypes and only then interpreted them through the tetrad [2].
- Three design features block testing: no coding rule or agreement statistic [3], no time horizon for reversal [10], and a universal claim that no artefact can fail [8].
- The best experimental analogue, Sparrow, Liu and Wegner's *Science* studies of the Google effect, tested one extension-and-amputation claim [12]. It did not replicate in the 2018 Camerer et al. multi-study project or in Hesselmann's 2020 follow-up [17].

## Details

### 1. What the four laws actually say: wording, structure and worked examples from the 1975 announcement to Laws of Media (1988)

The tetrad is four questions that can be put to any human artefact. Library and Archives Canada's McLuhan exhibition, drawing on *Laws of Media* (1988), gives the canonical wording: "1. What does it enhance? 2. What does it make obsolete? 3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier? 4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?" [1] The four are conventionally named enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal, and the sequence of the questions is not a sequence in time.

The archive is explicit that the four hold at once, and that McLuhan's own loose talk about them succeeding one another was a slip rather than the doctrine: "It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order." [1] That simultaneity matters for how the tetrad can be assessed. A set of four simultaneous descriptions of one artefact is not a sequence of predictions, so a failure in one quadrant cannot be read as a failed forecast about the next.

Two features of the questions do real work. Obsolescence names what the new form pushes aside, and retrieval names an older form it brings back; both are about the relation between the new medium and what came before it [1]. Reversal is conditional: it describes what happens "when pushed to extremes", not what happens next [1]. The general form is that a medium at its limit produces the opposite of its own gift.

The same archive insists the tetrad is not a scientific instrument. It quotes *Laws of Media* (p. 116) calling the tetrad a tool for exploring the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool for describing situations in process rather than settled ones [1]. The archive attributes those words to the book. They sit awkwardly against the same book's opening claim to be offering testable and falsifiable laws (section 2).

The tension is inside the book, not imported by later critics. Francesco Guardiani surveyed roughly thirty reviews of *Laws of Media* for *McLuhan Studies* at the University of Toronto. He records that the introduction calls the laws "the single biggest intellectual discovery of the last couple of centuries" [15]. On page 7 of the same book they are described as a "heuristic" device "that allows for adjustments and implementations" [15]. Guardiani also reports William Kuhns's reading of the four slots as "the metaphysical coda of McLuhan's career" [15]. On that reading the tetrad is the summary statement of a body of work rather than a method inside it [15].

The questions survive in applied form largely because they are easy to operationalise as prompts. Michael Bolton's "McLuhan for Testers" column in *Better Software* (October 2007) tells software testers that "McLuhan proposed that every medium can be submitted to fourprobes—testing heuristics— that he called the Laws of Media" [13]. He then puts them to a requirement, a feature or an organisational change: what does it extend, what does it obsolesce, what earlier medium does it retrieve, and how does it reverse when stretched [13]. His worked examples are the camera-phone and a dedicated software test team. The phone's retrieval question surfaces the Pony Express, the all-in-one printer-scanner-fax and the Tamagotchi [13]. Its reversal question surfaces interrupted conversation and the desk that follows you everywhere [13]. This is the tetrad's most common afterlife: not a law but a four-prompt checklist for anticipating unintended effects.

What the four questions are *not* is a specification. None of them tells the analyst how much of an effect counts, over what period, or against what baseline [1]. That absence is a fact about the questions as worded, not a verdict the sources concede. The McLuhans offered the tetrad as science and invoked Popper to certify it, so the charge that it cannot fail is a criticism of the scheme rather than a property its authors accepted (section 4).

Reviewers of the book saw the problem at the time. Guardiani's survey records John Sturrock's verdict that "The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing" [15]. It also records John Fekete's objection that the number four is treated as a "metaphysically privileged explanatory structure", with no grounds given for privileging it [15]. Those are objections to the tetrad's form rather than to any particular application, and they arrived with the book.

### 2. What status the McLuhans claimed for the tetrad — science, Popperian falsifiability, definitional necessity, and the retreat to analogy

The McLuhans asked for the tetrad to be read as science, in the specific Popperian sense of testable and falsifiable claims. The opening of *Laws of Media* states it directly: "This essay offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws) observations about the structure and nature of things man makes and does" [7]. The publisher's description follows the book's own framing, calling the four laws "a new scientific basis for media studies, testable, and able to allow for prediction" [8].

The same publisher's text contains the sentence that undoes the claim: "Inherent in every human innovation is an answer to each of the questions of this tetrad; anything that does not contain answers to these four questions is not the product of human creation." [8] If answering all four is a condition of being a human artefact at all, then no artefact can fail the tetrad. A test that nothing can fail is not a test. This is not a hostile reading imposed from outside. It is the definitional claim and the falsifiability claim printed on the same page of the same description, and they cannot both be true in the ordinary sense of "falsifiable."

Popper is the right comparison, and it has been made explicitly. Eduardo Basbaum, writing in *ARS* (2019), argues the tetrad fails Popper's own criterion in the way Popper said Freudian psychoanalysis fails it: "It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands, since its testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper dismisses Freudian psychoanalysis theory: it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim." [7] A scheme that always works explains nothing, because it excludes nothing.

The most interesting defence is not that the tetrad is testable after all, but that it is a claim about a different kind of cause. Eric McLuhan's later statement in *Explorations in Media Ecology* places the laws under formal cause rather than efficient cause: "Formal cause, however, remains enigmatic. Long thought to be “plans” or “blueprints,” it is found to be situational or environmental cause and to operate in many fields, particularly the arts, and the study of media and their ecologies." [11] On this reading the tetrad does not predict what a maker will do. It describes the situation in which the making happens. The appropriate test of a description of a situation is whether it illuminates, not whether it predicts. That reframing rescues the tetrad from the falsifiability charge by giving up the claim that generated the charge.

Institutional reception took the same route. Library and Archives Canada states flatly that "The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool" [1]. That is a fact about the tetrad's standing. The custodian of McLuhan's papers presents the four laws as an exploratory instrument, not as the new science the book's title announces [1].

There is a third position, which is that McLuhan never meant the scientific framing to be taken literally and used it as one more probe. Bolton's account of McLuhan's method is that ambiguity was deliberate: "His own words and ideas were often confusing and contradictory, but this was deliberate. Rather than rejecting ambiguity, McLuhan embraced it. His intent was to probe—to investigate and explore ideas with think- ing tools that included metaphor, paradox, and even satire" [10]. That is a defensible reading of McLuhan's rhetoric. It is not a defence of the sentence on page 3 of *Laws of Media*. It converts the book's central methodological claim into a rhetorical gesture, which is what the critics say it was.

Two structural problems remain whatever status is claimed. The four laws are asserted to hold simultaneously, and Library and Archives Canada concedes that McLuhan himself sometimes spoke of them as succeeding each other [1]. The tetrad is also offered as universally applicable, to any artefact at any time [8]. That universality makes it valuable as a probe, and makes it unfalsifiable as a law [8]. The most that can be said for the scientific claim is that the McLuhans wanted a science of formal cause and had no method for one. The least is that they attached the vocabulary of Popper to a scheme built to be unfalsifiable.

### 3. How scholars applied and extended the tetrad after 1988: Levinson's wheels, Logan's new media, Strate and media ecology, Harman's metaphysics, the Lost Tetrads

The tetrad's post-1988 literature is overwhelmingly application, not assessment. It divides into four streams: anthropologists and communication scholars using it on new media, McLuhan's collaborators systematising it, philosophers annexing it, and practitioners using it as a checklist.

The earliest extended trial was by an anthropologist. Thomas Hylland Eriksen, at the University of Oslo, applied the tetrad to the Internet in 1996 and treated the four laws as a starting point rather than a result: "Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out." [4] He filled in tetrads for CD-ROM, the LP, the aeroplane and the Internet. He called the results "questionable" illustrations whose value was in forcing distinctions between technological, social and cultural levels of effect [4]. The Internet tetrad is the most revealing thing in his paper: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics." [4] A scheme that assigns the same phenomenon to all four slots is being used as a set of prompts, not as a set of claims about the world.

Peer-reviewed applications followed the same pattern. Isabelle Adam's 2016 paper in *Glocality* applies the tetrad to the smartphone, and her defence of the method is its universality rather than its accuracy: "Although McLuhan developed the tetrad three decades ago, it is universal in nature and therefore still applicable to present and future technological developments." [3] The filled-in result treats enhancement as access and speed, obsolescence as feature phones, personal computers and home printers, and retrieval as cameras and books: "The smartphone enhances the accessibility and convenience of the medium internet, which also accelerates the speed of real-time communication." [3] Adam concedes the interpretive latitude explicitly: "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions." [3] She also claims only that the tetrad lets the analyst "try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [3].

The most ambitious extension is Robert K. Logan's attempt to convert the tetrad into a component of a general theory. Logan argues that "despite McLuhan’s claim not to have a theory of communication that in fact the body of his work does indeed constitute a theory of media and their effects which I have called his General Theory of Media (GToM) that also includes his Laws of Media (LoM)" [14]. His paper then does something the earlier applications avoid: it compares "three notions of law: i. McLuhan’s notion of law as used in his Laws of Media; ii. the notions of the Law in the legal sense and iii. the notion of law as formulated in scientific laws." [14] That comparison, from the most sympathetic systematiser, concedes that the tetrad's "law" is not the scientific kind. The paper is a preprint [14]. It may indicate where sympathetic scholarship is heading, and it is not a peer-reviewed statement.

New primary material also kept appearing, which is itself a form of extension. "The Missing Media Laws," by Marshall and Eric McLuhan, was published in *Explorations in Media Ecology* volume 6, issue 3, in September 2007, pages 197 to 202 [9]. It appeared in a media-ecology journal, which is where the tetrad's unpublished material has appeared since [9]. A 2017 collection, *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan*, gathers further tetrads. Its contents could not be read in this pass, so the report does not characterise them.

Philosophy took the tetrad up on different terms. Graham Harman's "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (in *New Waves in Philosophy of Technology*, 2009) argues the tetrad applies to all objects rather than only human artefacts. Later work follows him. A 2018 article in *Explorations in Media Ecology* on screens as media opens by invoking "Graham Harman in the charge that Marshall and Eric McLuhan’s laws of media are applicable beyond human-made artefacts", then extends the framework to the screen as a material object. That move increases the tetrad's scope and, by the same stroke, removes the last constraint that might have made it fail on some object. Harman's chapter itself could not be read in full within this pass, so his argument is reported here at the level of its theses and its reception rather than its text.

Practice is the fourth stream, and it is the largest. Bolton's *Better Software* column is the clearest specimen: it treats a test team as a medium, argues the team enhances the project's ability to learn about the product, obsolesces the field technician and the careful developer, and reverses into the team not reporting what it finds [13]. The team also retrieves an older role, which Bolton names as the test pilot, the food taster, the editor and the lab researcher [13]. The column is a competent use of the four questions on a novel object, and it demonstrates the tetrad's real transferable strength. It makes an analyst look at a thing's effects instead of its content. It also demonstrates the weakness. Every one of those four assignments is a plausible reading with no evidence attached and no rival reading ruled out.

One recent peer-reviewed application shows the retrospective mechanics at work. Takkeci and Erdem's 2024 study of online architectural studios during the pandemic screened 176 records and coded 20 empirical papers [2]. The coding scheme was not the tetrad: the authors sorted the findings under four studio archetypes, and only then read them through the tetrad — "This process was followed by organizing the findings and interpreting them within the tetradic framework" [2]. A single finding then does multiple duty: "Hence, the idea of the community of practices reversed into isolated individuals, and the multidimensional communication of the studio was obsolesced, and this retrieved the master apprenticeship pedagogy because the tutor ended up as the only actor through whom all the exchanges happen" [2]. The authors assign three quadrants to that one observed shift, after the fact [2]. No independent measure separates the three. The authors' own framing concedes the point: "McLuhan’s ideas on media can be viewed as an evolutionary theory that needs to be re-evaluated with each technological transformation." [2]

### 4. The criticism: Venable's 1976 exchange, 'Flaws in McLuhan's Laws', Tyler's Procrustean probe, and the unfalsifiability charge

The critique arrived before the book did. In 1976 *Technology and Culture* carried both halves of an exchange: W. H. Venable's "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and McLuhan's reply, "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" [5]. The reply's title is the argument: the critic had misunderstood. Both items are behind paywalls and could not be read in full in this pass. What is known here of Venable's case is its existence, its title and its venue rather than its content, which is a real limit on this section.

The most rigorous published critique is Tom Tyler's "Play: A Procrustean Probe," a conference paper in the DiGRA Digital Library (2007). Tyler states the McLuhans' claim in its strongest form in order to reject it. He reports Eric McLuhan's claim in *Laws of Media* that the questions can be asked, and the answers checked, by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact [6]. His answer is flat: "This is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans’ own examples illustrates." [6]

The illustration is the book's own inconsistency. On the same page of *Laws of Media*, the McLuhans give two different tetrads for wine. The second version: "In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult." [6] Tyler draws the inference: "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad’s application, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by “anyone, anywhere, at any time”." [6] Reproducibility fails at the source, before any external replication is attempted.

Tyler's objection is a double bind rather than a charge of vagueness. The tetrad is too loose and too rigid at once: "Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit. At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps." [6] The looseness means any set of answers can be defended; the rigidity means answers must be produced even where the evidence is absent. Together they describe a scheme that cannot be wrong and cannot be empty.

Tyler does not conclude that the tetrad is worthless, and his concession is the most useful part of the paper for anyone who wants to keep using it. He treats it as a heuristic that directs attention to a medium's operation rather than its content. His own application is uneven, and he says so. Parts of his reversal quadrant are his own argument rather than cited research, and he calls one retrieval claim something that "will remain, I suspect, a moot point." The standard he demonstrates is therefore a discipline rather than a formula, and it is not a test.

The unfalsifiability charge has a second route, through Popper. Basbaum's 2019 *ARS* article makes the comparison to psychoanalysis, though as a debatable judgement rather than a verdict: "It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands" [7]. The two critiques converge from different directions. Tyler shows that the tetrad cannot be applied reproducibly. Basbaum argues that it probably cannot be refuted, since it "seems to always work" [7]. Taken together they make the scientific claim hard to sustain, and Basbaum's own hedge is a reminder that this is an argument about a criterion, not a measurement.

There is a defence, and it is worth stating at full strength. The tetrad's defenders do not claim reproducibility. They claim the four questions surface effects that other framings miss, and that a diversity of answers is the point rather than a defect. Eric McLuhan's formal-cause framing gives this position a philosophical footing: the laws describe "situational or environmental cause" rather than a maker's plan [11]. Whether that framing implies that agreement between analysts does not matter is a further step, and the passage does not say so; the inference is this report's. On that account the wine problem is not a refutation but an illustration of the method's fertility. The defence has a cost, which is that it gives up the testability claim the book opens with [7].

The debate's centre of gravity has shifted over fifty years, and the shift is the finding. In 1976 a critic published "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and McLuhan replied that the laws had been misunderstood [5]. By 1988 the publisher was advertising the book as testable while also saying that anything without answers to the four questions "is not the product of human creation" [8]. By 2007 the most careful critic could treat the tetrad as a valuable probe that is not science [6]. By 2016 an applier could describe its output as "at least speculation" without embarrassment [3]. The scientific claim has not been refuted so much as retired by its own users.

### 5. Has anyone tested it empirically? Direct attempts, operationalisations, adjacent quantitative tests, and what the tetrad's design permits

No study has been found that tests the tetrad as the McLuhans described it. The search covered the journals that carry tetrad work (*Explorations in Media Ecology*, *Glocality*, *McLuhan Studies*, *New Explorations*), the DiGRA library, and the recent peer-reviewed applications. What exists is a body of applied tetrads and no controlled test of the four laws as hypotheses. That negative finding is the answer to the question. It is very likely rather than certain, since a test published outside media studies, or in a language other than English, could have been missed.

The closest thing to an empirical tetrad study organises other people's data rather than generating its own. Takkeci and Erdem (2024) screened 176 records on online architectural studios during the pandemic and read 20 empirical papers, coding them under studio archetypes before interpreting the results through the tetrad [2][2]. The authors state the framework's basis plainly: "As referred to in this paper, the functionality of the tetrad is not based on theoretical grounds, but revolves around four questions based on empirical observation" [2]. That is the tetrad as an interpretive frame over findings, not as an object of measurement. The paper's limitations section concedes the ceiling: the review "relied solely on previously published research" and generated no new measurements [2].

The applied literature itself explains why a test has not been run. Three design features block it.

First, the tetrad admits multiple defensible answers for the same object, by its users' own account. Adam's smartphone paper states that "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions." [3] A test needs a coding rule independent analysts can apply to the same artefact, and a measure of whether they agree. No tetrad study located here reports an inter-coder reliability statistic for quadrant assignment.

Second, the reversal law has no stated time horizon. Bolton's restatement makes the timing explicit: reversal effects "are emergent; they may be apparent immediately, or they may not be realized until the figure fades into the ground and becomes ubiquitous." [10] A prediction that a medium will flip into its opposite at some unspecified point cannot be scored as right or wrong at any particular date. The same passage also shows the escape hatch: if the reversal has not happened yet, the medium is simply not yet ubiquitous.

Third, the claims are stated in a form that cannot fail. The publisher's own description says that anything which does not contain answers to the four questions "is not the product of human creation" [8]. A universal existential claim of that shape is true of every artefact by construction.

Where the tetrad's content has been tested, it has been tested under other names, by researchers who were not testing McLuhan. The best example is the Google-effects work. Betsy Sparrow, Jenny Liu and Daniel Wegner's four studies in *Science* (2011) found that when people expect future access to information, they recall less of the content and more of where to find it [12]. That is an operationalised, falsifiable version of the claim that a medium extends one faculty and amputates another. The authors frame it through transactive memory, not the tetrad, and it tests one effect on memory rather than the four laws [12]. It is also a warning about the standard of evidence involved. The key effect did not replicate in the 2018 Camerer et al. multi-study project covering 21 studies from *Nature* and *Science* [17]. Hesselmann's 2020 study, designed to follow Sparrow's own methodological advice, also found no evidence [17]. The original also had unresolved statistical problems: unclear sample size, post hoc word selection and single-trial measures [17]. Even a single testable fragment of McLuhan-style thinking, taken out of the tetrad and given a proper experiment, has proved fragile.

Adjacent evidence of the same kind is available for particular quadrants, and a programme of testing could be built on it. Media-multitasking research tests whether a medium's enhancement comes at a cost to another capacity. Displacement studies test obsolescence by measuring time reallocated between media. Retrieval claims are testable as formal or stylistic revivals, measurable in content corpora. Reversal claims are the hardest, because the theory does not say when the flip occurs [10]. What is missing is not measurement technique but a decision about what would count as the tetrad being wrong.

The most useful attempt to supply that missing decision is not empirical but conceptual. Tyler's argument that the tetrad is a probe rather than a science converts it from a claim into a procedure for generating claims [6]. The outputs of that procedure are then testable one at a time, as ordinary hypotheses about specific media. That is the only route to empirical work the sources support: not testing the tetrad as a whole, but testing the individual effect claims it generates, while reporting where a quadrant cannot be filled.

One 2018 conference paper shows the teaching use: "This paper summarizes how the McLuhan Tetrad help the students to handle the laser cleaning technique as a case of study." [18] The smartphone paper is the same pattern in research form, structuring an assessment whose substance comes from elsewhere [3]. Neither claims to have tested the tetrad. Across the literature reviewed here, the tetrad functions as a prompt set, and the empirical question it raises has been answered by substitution: the four questions get tested one at a time, by other fields, under other names, or not at all.


## Beyond this question

The finding that matters for anyone using the tetrad is that no version of it has ever been scored. A tetrad analysis currently produces no artefact that can later be marked wrong. The cheapest remedy is procedural and costs nothing: state, for each quadrant, what observation would show it false, and record the quadrants where no such observation exists. Tyler's wine example shows why this is worth doing. The McLuhans produced two incompatible answers on one page, so the disagreement was available at the moment of writing and was not recorded [6].

The second implication is about aggregation. Run four questions over a hundred artefacts and every one produces four plausible answers. The exercise then generates a hundred prompt sets and zero findings. Findings appear only when a single quadrant claim is separated out and tested, as the memory literature did with the extension-and-amputation idea. That fragment then failed replication [17]. Anyone treating tetrad output as a stock of established claims is over-reading the method by a wide margin.

The record already holds a research document that reaches a compatible conclusion from the same evidence, arguing that the tetrad should be run as rival hypotheses with empty quadrants permitted and a dated stake attached. This report supplies the prior question that proposal assumes: there is no baseline of successful tetrad tests to compare against, because the literature contains applications and no test.

## Open questions

No controlled test of the four laws was located. This is the central gap. The report's negative answer is very likely rather than certain, since a test published outside media studies, in another language, or in a book not indexed by the sources searched here could have been missed. Nothing in the literature reviewed claims such a test exists. That is weaker evidence than a systematic search of every relevant bibliography would be.

The 1976 exchange could not be read. Venable's "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and McLuhan's reply "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws" are behind a paywall, so Venable's actual argument is unexamined here, as distinct from its title and its existence [5]. This is the single largest hole in section 4. Secondary accounts describe Venable reading the laws through Peirce's logic of signs, and McLuhan replying that the tetrads are analogical rather than logical. No primary text was read in this pass, so that account is not reported as a finding.

Graham Harman's chapter on the McLuhans and metaphysics was not read in full. Section 3 reports his claim that the tetrad applies to all objects at the level of theses and reception rather than text. A reader who wants the strongest philosophical defence of the tetrad should go to the chapter itself.

*The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan* (2017) was not read. How many tetrads it contains, whether Eric McLuhan's editorial apparatus discusses failures, and whether any tetrad in it was abandoned because a quadrant came out empty are all unknown. Eric McLuhan is reported to have said his father searched for a fifth law and for a single case where one of the four did not apply; that claim is not verified here.

Nobody has built the obvious instrument. A testable tetrad would need a fixed coding protocol, two or more independent analysts, a reported agreement statistic, a stated time horizon for reversal, and a pre-registered list of observations that would count against each quadrant. No such protocol exists in the literature located here, and the reversal timing problem is the hardest part: a reversal that has not happened can always be deferred to a later date [10].

Two coverage notes. Several sources used here are open-access articles that quote the same canonical wording of the four questions, so the apparent agreement on wording reflects a shared source rather than independent corroboration [1][8]. And the applied literature is heavily weighted to sympathetic users: the critics who dismissed the tetrad outright are represented mainly through a survey of reviews [15], not through their own texts.
