[13] A youth employment "fall" is therefore not by itself evidence about hiring, which is why the crux section turns on which comparison identifies the effect.

Haanwinckel shows that the standard exposure designs can mislead: [7] "Using theory, simulations, and evidence from Brazil, I show when these approaches can mislead and how their performance depends on specification choices." [7] Neumark and Wascher add that apparent patterns in the literature may reflect a genuine change over time rather than publication bias: [8] "We present results indicating that the evidence is more consistent with a change in the estimated minimum wage effect over time than with publication bias.

More generally, we demonstrate that existing approaches to testing for publication bias may generate spurious evidence of such bias when there are structural changes in some parameters." [8] A Canadian claim about 2017-2019 is exactly the case where the effect could differ from the 1981-2011 panels that dominate Canadian work.

The strongest case for the thesis rests on four kinds of evidence: a peer-reviewed Canadian estimate from the largest provincial shock, a Canadian meta-analytic teenage elasticity, national labour force data from the quarters when the rises took effect, and an official forecast made before the rises happened. **Alberta is the best Canadian test, and it finds losses among the young.** Alberta legislated a 47% increase over three years, reaching a $15 floor [22].

Fossati and Marchand study the episode with a synthetic control on Labour Force Survey data, and they report that [22] "Employment losses occurred at similar elasticities, but with large level changes, mostly among younger workers." [22] The design matters. [22]

"Alberta is the first North American province, state, or territory to have this $15 minimum wage, with an unexpectedly large increase (47%) occurring over a short time horizon (3 years)." [22] Most minimum wage studies are identified on small, expected changes.
Over it, [9] "youth part-time employment dropped by 6 percent while Albertans aged 25 and over experienced a less than one percent decline.

During the same period a year earlier, part-time employment increased for adults and decreased for young people by about one percent." [9] The prior year moving the opposite way is what makes this more than a level difference.
The same analyst states the premise the whole "for" case rests on: [9] "It is well understood that minimum wage increases hit youth (15-24) harder than the rest of population.

This is mainly because young people are less experienced and tend to have a part-time, low-paying jobs." [9] **The Canadian meta-analytic estimate for teenagers is negative and not an artefact of publication selection.** Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature reports, for the group most exposed to the floor, [19] "For teenagers, the demographic group with the largest share of minimum wage workers and thus providing the findings of most interest to policy-makers and legislators, I find no evidence of a publication bias" [19] and puts the size at [19] "a minimum wage elasticity of about −0.27" [19].
A −0.27 elasticity means a 10% rise in the floor implies roughly a 2.7% fall in teen employment, a calculation from [19].

That matters because the post-2017 provincial increases were large by historical standards, which is what made the Bank of Canada expect measurable losses [15]. **Statistics Canada's own review found the effect, and found it concentrated on teenagers.** The agency's analytical article concludes that total employment is roughly unaffected but that [1] "Rather, an increase in the minimum wage would seem to be associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers," [1] and gives the magnitude as [1] "The effect on employment varies between 3% and 6%, depending on the study." [1] The agency adds that effects are larger when the floor approaches 50% of average hourly earnings — the condition the post-2017 increases created in several provinces. **National data in the year the largest rises took effect show an age-specific youth decline.** In November 2018, after the largest provincial increases had come into force [16], Statistics Canada reported a year-over-year fall in youth employment of 61,000, or 2.4%, and called it [18] "the largest year-over-year decrease since July 2016" [18].
The decline was not part of a general slump: in the same release, core-aged employment rose. [18]

"In the 12 months to November, employment within this age group rose by 208,000 (+1.7%), largely the result of gains for women (+129,000)." [18] An age-specific fall while prime-age employment grows is the pattern a youth wage floor predicts. **The official forecast, made before the fact, was for job losses.** The Bank of Canada's December 2017 staff analytical note on the scheduled provincial increases projected: [15] "A structural general equilibrium simulation suggests that minimum wage increases would reduce the level of gross domestic product by roughly 0.1 per cent by early 2019 and boost CPI inflation by about 0.1 pp.

While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000)." [15] This is a model simulation, not a measurement, and the 60,000 figure is economy-wide rather than youth-specific.

It therefore supports the thesis only indirectly, by showing that a central bank expected the increases to cost measurable numbers of jobs. **The employer-side account adds a mechanism.** The Canadian Federation of Independent Business frames youth hiring as a cost decision and asks for offsetting relief: [10] "Lower the cost of hiring youth: Reduce payroll taxes or offer targeted incentives (e.g., EI premium holidays, refundable tax credits) to encourage small businesses to bring on young workers." [10] That is evidence of how employers say they respond, not an estimate of how many jobs were lost.

Fossati and Marchand report regional employment losses in four of the five non-urban economic regions, but not in Alberta's two main cities, which they describe as showing the significance and nuance of regional heterogeneity [22].

Second, the strongest advocacy version of the claim is commentary, not estimation: the Fraser Institute's labour policy material links a wage floor to a provincial youth unemployment rate — [11] "Youth unemployment in the province hit 14.1 per cent in July." [11] — without a counterfactual.

The CFIB's survey of youth and small business finds that [10] "More than a third would be unwilling to look for jobs that are mainly outdoors and exposed to weather conditions, or jobs that pay at or near minimum wage." [10] If a third of young people will not take a minimum-wage job at all, then weak youth employment is at least partly a matching problem about job quality, scheduling and location rather than a shortage of openings created by a wage floor.

Their central finding: [21] "When we implement our estimator for Job Leavers, we find no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes." [21] The authors are explicit that this is a rejection, not a null: [21] "Thus, this result (plus the existence of a spike at the minimum wage) rejects standard neoclassical models and is potentially problematic for other models as well." [21] A minimum wage rise that leaves the wage distribution of leavers unchanged is a rise that is not pushing low-paid workers out of jobs.

Firms appear to anchor their internal wage structure on the floor: [21] "Our findings are consistent with a model where entry wages are set according to a job ladder, and where firms anchor their internal wage structure on the minimum wage due to fairness or internal incentives issues." [21] On this account a higher floor shifts the whole lower part of the entry-wage distribution right.

This is the strongest alternative explanation the thesis must defeat, and it is an inference from Canadian data rather than a hypothesis. **The Canadian estimate of no effect is not an outlier — the international summaries are small.** Dube's review for HM Treasury concludes: [12] "Overall the most up to date body of research from US, UK and other developed countries points to a very muted effect of minimum wages on employment, while significantly increasing the earnings of low paid workers.

Importantly, this was found to be the case even for the most recent ambitious policies." [12] The own-wage elasticity meta-analysis puts a number on "muted": [2] "We find that most studies to date suggest a fairly modest impact of minimum wages on jobs: the median OWE estimate of 72 studies published in academic journals is -0.13, which suggests that only around 13 percent of the potential earnings gains from minimum wage increases are offset due to associated job losses.
Estimates published since 2010 tend to be closer to zero." [2] Two further bounds follow from the size of the directly affected group.

In Canada, only a small minority of employees are paid at the floor — Statistics Canada reports the size of the directly affected group: [1] "Between 1997 and 2013, the proportion of employees paid at minimum wage increased from 5.0% to 6.7%." [1] A policy affecting under a tenth of employees can move aggregate youth employment only modestly, unless the effect on the directly affected group is very large.
That is a calculation from [1]. **The youth employment decline begins in 2023, not 2017.** This is the decisive timing fact.

Statistics Canada reports that through 2024 the youth employment rate fell, [24] "continuing a downward trend that began in April 2023" [24], and that by December 2024 the youth employment rate stood 4.4 percentage points below its 2017-to-2019 pre-pandemic average of 58.2% [24].

Statistics Canada reports: [23] "The unemployment rate for returning students has increased each summer since 2022 (when it was 10.4%)." [23] For summer 2025 the returning-student unemployment rate was 17.9%, the highest since summer 2009 outside the pandemic year [23].
And the youth unemployment rate in August 2025 was 14.5%, after July's rate came in as the highest since September 2010 [23].

Every one of these deteriorations is a 2022-to-2025 phenomenon. **In the years the rises actually took effect, youth employment was growing.** The May 2019 Labour Force Survey, released after the largest provincial increases had come into force [16], reported that [17] "On a year-over-year basis, youth employment rose by 64,000 (+2.6%)." [17] Within that, the group most exposed to a youth wage floor did best: [17] "Compared with 12 months earlier, employment among 20- to 24-year-old students grew by 32,000 (+7.4%) in May, as a result of an increase in part-time work." [17] If the 2017-2019 increases had reduced youth employment, this is the release where the reduction should be visible.

It is not. **A rival cause with the right timing: school enrolment.** A Canadian study of 136 provincial minimum wage amendments finds that higher floors move young people between schooling options rather than only between jobs: [20] "Quantitatively, a 10% increase in the minimum wage increases community-college enrollment by 6% and reduces university enrollment by 5%." [20] The labour force survey counts enrolled students who are not working as outside employment.

This is a competing explanation for a youth employment fall, not a refutation of one. **An independent official evaluation reached the opposite conclusion about youth rates.** The UK Low Pay Commission, which sets youth sub-minimum rates and has watched youth labour-market outcomes deteriorate, states: [4] "While the Commission recognises that labour market outcomes for young people have deteriorated over the past two years, we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls." [4] Its place-based test points away from the thesis: [4] "If the increases to the youth rates were damaging youth employment, we would expect to see bigger falls in the areas with higher youth coverage rates.

However, the chart shows that even over the period where youth rates have been rising at least as fast as the NLW, we find the opposite – youth employment fell more in areas with the lowest youth coverage and the largest falls in youth employee numbers have been in London where youth coverage is low." [4] This is a different country, and its institutions differ — the UK has a youth sub-minimum and Canada largely does not — so it bears on the general mechanism rather than directly on Canada. **How the two cases compare.** The "for" case has one peer-reviewed Canadian estimate with youth-specific losses, one Canadian meta-analytic elasticity, one national data point from 2018, and one official forecast.

Haanwinckel shows that the two standard exposure designs — the effective-minimum-wage design and the fraction-affected design — can mislead, and that their results depend on specification: [7] "Using theory, simulations, and evidence from Brazil, I show when these approaches can mislead and how their performance depends on specification choices." [7] The reason is that provinces raising their floor sharply are rarely a random sample.
It found the opposite [4]: youth employment fell more in areas with the lowest youth coverage, and most in London, where coverage is low.

The Commission itself notes that population and migration dynamics may matter in London [4]. **The outcome measure is the second crux.** "Employment" can mean a headcount, an employment rate, or hours, and the three move differently.
Statistics Canada's own note on the problem is explicit: changes in an age group's employment mix genuine hiring changes with ageing and migration in and out of the band [17].
The Commission reports that [4] "Despite the large increase in coverage in 2025, effective coverage fell.

It may be that effective coverage is not particularly sensitive to changes in the youth rates, instead being driven by other factors, such as compositional changes to the youth workforce and changes to the NLW rate." [4] So the measure of how many young workers are bound by the floor is itself driven by composition.

It may mean no effect, or it may mean the floor was not binding on the workers being counted. **Whether the floor binds at all is the third crux, and it is the one the Canadian case cannot yet settle.** The IZA review states the problem plainly: [6] "However, there are studies that show no employment effects of minimum wages and an occasional study that shows a positive effect.

Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective." [6] A null result in a province whose floor was already below the youth market wage tells us nothing about the thesis.

This is why the size of the post-2017 increases matters: a 47% rise over three years in Alberta [22] is the kind of change that makes the floor bind, whereas a small indexed adjustment may not. **The method dispute is the fourth crux, and it is where the two best Canadian studies diverge.** Fossati and Marchand use a synthetic control on provincial aggregates and find youth losses [22].
Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend use worker-level turnover and find no excess separations below the new floor [21].
This is exactly the hiring channel Statistics Canada described [1].

The turnover study is the more relevant test of the neoclassical layoff story, and the thesis does not require layoffs. **What the crux shows so far.** The one Canadian study that tests the relevant margin, at the relevant scale, in the relevant period, finds youth employment losses [22].
But it covers a single province, and its effect vanishes in that province's two largest cities [22].

Haanwinckel's work supplies the reason for care in specifying it: [7] "Using theory, simulations, and evidence from Brazil, I show when these approaches can mislead and how their performance depends on specification choices." [7] No such study has been published.

The Canadian literature that exists uses panels ending in 2011, or worker-level turnover over 1997-2016 [21], or a single-province synthetic control [22]. **A demonstration that the post-2017 floors were not binding on youth wages.** If the share of young workers paid at or near the floor did not rise when the floor rose, then any null finding is uninformative rather than exculpatory.

The IZA review warns that a null result has two possible meanings: [6] "Findings of no effect are consistent with a minimum wage that is below the market wage and therefore is ineffective." [6] A modelling study reaches a related conclusion — that the disemployment result follows from the floor being binding, since [14] "binding minimum wages increase the unemployment rate of both low and high-productivity workers" [14].

The Bank of Canada's 2017 note establishes that the scheduled increases were expected to bind economy-wide [15], but no published Canadian study reports the youth-specific bite of the post-2017 provincial floors, which is the measure that would settle it. **A replication of the turnover test on post-2017 data.** Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend's test is the kind that would detect displacement if it existed.
But their window ends in December 2016 [21], and their finding is that [21] "minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage" [21].

This is the most valuable missing piece of evidence, because it addresses the hiring-versus-layoff ambiguity identified in section 4. **A test that separates the wage floor from the competing causes.** The UK Commission has committed to precisely this, and describes the confound it faces: [4] "Outcomes for young people are largely driven by the recent trends in the industries in which they work.
Hospitality and retail are particularly important as they are the largest employers of young people." [4] For Canada, the same confound has an obvious local form.

Youth employment began falling in April 2023 [24], a period of rapid population growth and of a construction and retail slowdown, and the summer student unemployment rate rose in every year from 2022 [23].

Any study that attributes the 2023-2025 decline to wage floors set in 2018 must first rule out those forces. **What the UK's own test implies for the Canadian question.** The Commission's place-based analysis is the closest thing to a template for the missing Canadian study, and its result points away from the thesis [4].

It treats the question as open: [4] "However, this remains an important question to ask." [4] That is the right posture for the Canadian case too. **A change in the institutional setting would also change the prediction.** The IZA review finds that the negative youth effects shrink when young workers are carved out of the adult floor: [6] "It also shows that reducing or eliminating the minimum wage for young unskilled workers reduces these negative effects." [6] Canada is a useful test case because it has mostly not done this.

The federal minimum wage database notes that [16] "In most jurisdictions, these rates also apply to young workers." [16] A finding of no harm in a province with a youth sub-minimum would therefore be consistent with the thesis rather than contrary to it.

For teenagers, the reductions in hirings largely exceed the number of layoffs, which explains why there is a significant and negative effect on employment in this age group.
notes.claim: The mechanism the "for" case relies on: youth employment falls not through layoffs but through reduced hiring — a distinction that matters for how the effect shows up in the data (flows, not headcount cuts).

Estimates published since 2010 tend to be closer to zero.
notes.claim: Meta-analysis of 88 studies: median own-wage elasticity of employment is -0.13, and post-2010 estimates are closer to zero — so job losses offset only ~13% of earnings gains. Core "case against" evidence that effects are small.

notes.quote: Rather, an increase in the minimum wage would seem to be associated with a decrease in employment among teenagers,
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's analysts conclude that minimum-wage increases leave total employment roughly unchanged but are associated with lower teenage employment — the agency's own statement of the core effect, and the basis for focusing on youth rather than all workers.

notes.claim: Statistics Canada reports the size of the estimated teenage employment effect: 3% to 6% depending on the study, with larger effects when the minimum wage approaches 50% of average hourly earnings — the magnitude the "for" case must defend.

notes.claim: The UK Low Pay Commission — the body that sets youth subminimum rates — states that despite a two-year deterioration in youth labour-market outcomes it knows of no robust evidence that higher youth rates caused the falls, while conceding the question is still open. Cross-country comparator for how the same measure/identification problem is handled elsewhere.
